# Vercel Hosting Costs & Backend Security — Due Diligence for mapstack-us

## Part A: Vercel Hosting Costs

**1. Hobby (free) plan limits relevant to a backend** (per Vercel's own docs, updated 2026-06-16): 1,000,000 function invocations/mo, 4 Active CPU-hrs, 360 GB-hrs provisioned memory, up to 1,000,000 Edge Requests, ~100GB "Fast Data Transfer" (fair-use guideline), max function duration 300s. [Hobby plan docs](https://vercel.com/docs/plans/hobby) | [Fair Use Guidelines](https://vercel.com/docs/limits/fair-use-guidelines)

**Critical finding on commercial use**: Vercel's Fair Use Guidelines explicitly state Hobby is "restricted to non-commercial personal use only," and — contrary to some third-party blog summaries — **the official page says asking for donations DOES count as commercial usage**: *"Asking for Donations fall under commercial usage."* Any paid contributor writing code also triggers the commercial definition. If mapstack-us ever adds a donate/sponsor button, it needs to move to Pro ($20/user/mo). [Fair Use Guidelines — Commercial usage](https://vercel.com/docs/limits/fair-use-guidelines)

**2. What changes with a backend**: A static site consumes ~zero function allowance. Adding API routes for auth callbacks and DB writes starts consuming Function Invocations, Active CPU, and Provisioned Memory. For a small side project's realistic traffic, staying under 1M invocations/4 CPU-hrs is very likely — the forcing functions to upgrade are more often the *commercial-use clause* (donations, sponsorship) or *team features* (multiple collaborators) than raw usage. If usage does exceed fair-use, Pro costs $20/seat/mo baseline plus pay-as-you-go overage: $0.60/1M invocations, $0.128/Active-CPU-hr, $0.0106/GB-hr memory. [Fair Use Guidelines — pricing table](https://vercel.com/docs/limits/fair-use-guidelines)

**3. Multi-zone gotcha**: Because the parent site (tools.mdostal.com) proxies requests to mapstack-us via rewrites, bandwidth gets double-counted — both the parent zone and the mapstack-us zone serve the same bytes, eating into each project's own ~100GB Hobby bandwidth allowance faster than a single-zone app would. Function invocations aren't double-billed the same way (the zone that owns the function absorbs the invocation), but bandwidth is a real multi-zone tax to watch. [Multi-zone billing writeup](https://dev.to/matthewwilson/eliminating-additional-bandwidth-charges-for-multi-zone-sites-on-vercel-1k5a) | [Vercel: serving multiple projects under one domain](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/how-can-i-serve-multiple-projects-under-a-single-domain)

## Part B: Security Practices

**Secrets**: Server-only secrets must never use the `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix (Next.js inlines those into the client bundle at build time) and should be scoped per Vercel environment (Production/Preview/Development). The project's existing `pnpm test:secrets` (`scripts/secret-scan.mjs`) is a real, working gate — it scans git-tracked/untracked-not-ignored files *and* the built `.next` output for known key-format signatures (AWS, OpenAI-style, GitHub PAT, Slack, PEM blocks, JWT shape). It's a legitimate practice but **not sufficient alone**: it's pattern-based, so a generic DB password or a secret accidentally given a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix without a recognizable key format would slip through. Pair it with code-review discipline and the Next.js public/private env convention.

**SQL injection**: Moving from read-only client-side SQLite to writable server-side Postgres requires parameterized queries throughout (e.g., `$1`-style placeholders via `node-postgres`, or a query builder/ORM like Drizzle) — never string-concatenate user input into SQL.

**Rate limiting**: In-memory limiters don't survive serverless cold starts or multi-region execution; use a distributed store like Upstash Redis with `@upstash/ratelimit` (sliding-window) at the edge/middleware layer for public write endpoints. [Upstash rate limiting guide](https://upstash.com/blog/nextjs-ratelimiting)

**CSRF**: Next.js Server Actions get automatic Origin/Host header checking; plain Route Handlers (API routes) do **not** — mutating API routes need explicit Origin/Referer validation and `SameSite=Lax`/`Strict` cookies for session tokens. [Next.js security blog](https://nextjs.org/blog/security-nextjs-server-components-actions) | [CSRF in Next.js](https://vibeappscanner.com/vulnerability-in/csrf-nextjs)

**Postgres RLS**: matters most when a client can query the DB directly with a shared key (Supabase's pattern). With Neon accessed only from server-side API routes, the app itself is the sole DB client, so RLS is a defense-in-depth layer against a future BOLA-style bug in server code, not a hard requirement. [Neon RLS discussion](https://vibe-eval.com/safety/neon/) | [Supabase RLS docs](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security)

**GDPR at this scale**: A plain-language privacy policy stating what's collected (email, via the auth provider) and why, plus a way to request account/data deletion (honored within ~1 month per GDPR Art. 17), is the realistic minimum. [Art. 17 GDPR](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/) A cookie-consent banner is only needed if non-essential cookies (analytics/ads) are added — the auth session cookie itself is "strictly necessary" and typically doesn't require consent. Formal DPO appointment, a full Art. 30 records-of-processing register, and paid consent-management platforms are overkill for a hobby project. [EDPB SME guide](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/sme/find-practical-info/faq_en)

## Must-do vs Nice-to-have

**Must-do before adding any backend:**
- Confirm no donate/sponsor button ships while on Hobby (or budget for Pro's $20/mo)
- Parameterized queries only; no string-built SQL
- Keep secrets server-only, unprefixed, scoped per Vercel environment; keep `test:secrets` gate running in CI
- CSRF defense on any Route Handler that mutates state (Origin check + SameSite cookies)
- Basic privacy policy + account/data-deletion path once real accounts/emails exist

**Nice-to-have, can wait:**
- Distributed rate limiting (Upstash) — add once public write traffic is non-trivial
- Postgres RLS — valuable defense-in-depth, but lower priority while Neon is only reachable via server code
- Cookie-consent banner — only once non-essential (analytics/ads) cookies are added
- Formal DPO/Art. 30 register — not required at hobby scale
